strengths: The paper provides a valuable and precise taxonomy distinguishing performance universality, score universality, and minimizer universality — three notions that had been conflated or used inconsistently in prior literature — and uses this taxonomy to organize a large, carefully curated related-work table (Table 1) covering RMT, AMP, CGMT, and Lindeberg-based approaches.

The framework unifies and recovers several strands of the exact-asymptotics literature (e.g., Karoui et al. 2013, Bean et al. 2013, Donoho & Montanari 2016, Mai & Liao's LFMM equations) as special cases of a single fixed-point system (Theorem 4.4), which is a nontrivial synthesis effort documented explicitly in Appendix D and F.

Theorem 7.1 (covariance-adjusted subspace confinement) gives a clean, interpretable geometric result showing how anisotropic noise skews the direction of the asymptotic estimator mean away from the naive signal subspace, and directly explains the structural source of score non-Gaussianity.

The paper is empirically grounded with both controlled synthetic experiments (bimodal features, elastic loss) and a real-data example (MNIST), explicitly demonstrating cases where moment-matched Gaussian surrogates fail to predict both the score distribution and the generalization performance, which supports the paper's central qualitative claim.

The authors are transparent about the conjectural status of their central technical tool (Claim 4.1) and the minimizer-universality assumption (Assumption 4), clearly labeling downstream results as conditional rather than overclaiming full rigor.

Extensive proof appendix (25+ pages) with detailed derivations, stability lemmas, and an independent RMT-based consistency check (Appendix D.2) for the ridge regression case, lending some cross-validation to the fixed-point equations even where the general CGMT extension is unproven.
weaknesses: The paper's central technical device, the non-Gaussian extension of CGMT (Claim 4.1), is explicitly stated as a conjecture rather than a proven comparison principle; nearly all headline results (Theorem 4.3, Theorem 4.4, and consequently Theorem 3.3 and Corollary 5.1) are conditional on this unproven claim, which is a significant soundness gap for results labeled 'Theorem.'

A second load-bearing assumption, minimizer universality (Assumption 4), which underlies the main score-characterization result (Theorem 6.1), is also unproven within the paper; its justification is deferred to an unpublished, in-preparation manuscript (Louart, 2026), making an important part of the argument currently unverifiable by readers.

The chain of conditional derivations (conjecture ⇒ deterministic fixed point ⇒ assumption ⇒ score law) means the paper's rigor is considerably weaker than the theorem-heavy presentation suggests; the practical takeaway is closer to a well-motivated heuristic framework than a fully established theory, which should be reflected more starkly in how results are framed (e.g., via 'Conjecture' or 'Heuristic Claim' labeling rather than 'Theorem' with post-hoc caveats).

Numerical validation is somewhat limited in scale and diversity: the main synthetic experiment uses very small n=50, p=30, and the MNIST experiment is a single coarse binary grouping; broader validation (varying n/p ratios, more loss/regularizer combinations, quantitative error bars on how well theory tracks empirics as n grows) would strengthen confidence that the asymptotic predictions are accurate outside curated examples.

The presentation is very dense, with heavy notation and many interlocking assumptions/theorems distributed across a long appendix; a clearer high-level summary distinguishing which results are unconditional versus which depend on Claim 4.1/Assumption 4 (e.g., in a table) would substantially improve readability and help readers gauge the actual certainty of each claim.

The degree of genuine novelty relative to the already extensive prior literature summarized in Table 1 is somewhat incremental in places — the paper's main new contribution is the explicit conceptual disentanglement and a broader (though conjectural) unifying fixed-point system, rather than a fundamentally new proof technique or previously inaccessible regime.

strengths: The paper provides a clear conceptual contribution by explicitly disentangling three previously conflated notions of Gaussian universality (performance, score, minimizer universality), and situates the work carefully against a large body of prior literature via a detailed comparison table (Table 1).

The theoretical framework is broad: it recovers as special cases several known results (Dobriban & Wager ridge regression, Karoui et al./Bean et al. fixed-point equations, Mai & Liao's LFMM equations), which is a non-trivial consistency check and increases confidence in the correctness of the derivations despite their heuristic derivation route.

The paper gives an explicit, interpretable criterion for score (non-)universality: x^T*theta-hat is asymptotically Gaussian iff x^T*mu_* is Gaussian, and further localizes the source of non-Gaussianity to the structured component in signal-plus-noise models (Theorem 7.1), which is conceptually illuminating and actionable.

Numerical experiments (synthetic bimodal-feature teacher-student model and an MNIST-based classification task) directly illustrate the theoretical claims, showing concrete cases where moment-matched Gaussian surrogates fail to predict performance/score distributions while the theory succeeds.

The appendix includes a substantial and reasonably self-contained proof apparatus (concentration of the minimizer, quadratic universality of the regularizer, RMT consistency checks, and multiclass extension), which aids reproducibility of the theoretical claims.
weaknesses: The central technical engine of the paper (Claim 4.1, the extension of CGMT to non-Gaussian concentrated designs) is explicitly stated as a conjecture rather than a proven theorem; nearly all headline results (Theorems 4.3, 6.1, 7.1, Corollary 5.1) are conditional on this unproven comparison principle, which is a significant soundness limitation despite the honesty of the disclosure.

Assumption 4 (minimizer universality), which is needed for the score-level characterization in Section 6, is also unproven within the paper; the authors cite a companion paper 'under preparation' (Louart, 2026) as future justification, meaning a load-bearing assumption currently rests on an unpublished, unverifiable reference.

The empirical validation is fairly limited in scale and diversity: the main synthetic illustration uses small dimensions (p=30, n=50), and the single real-data experiment (binary MNIST subset) is relegated to the appendix with relatively brief description; broader real-world or larger-scale validation would strengthen confidence in the practical relevance of the theory.

The paper is dense with many stacked assumptions (Poincaré concentration, smoothness/strong convexity, weak-separability-type Assumption 3, saddle-point stability, uniform integrability) whose joint plausibility in realistic settings is not deeply discussed, making it hard for readers to assess when the theory's preconditions genuinely hold in practice.

Minor presentation issues remain, e.g., the 'Software and Data' section is truncated/incomplete in the manuscript, and some derivations (e.g., in Appendix C, Proposition C.2) rely on formal max-min interchanges 'assumed' to be valid without rigorous justification, compounding the conjectural nature of the framework.
